## Answer

For square matrices, Sylvester's determinant identity gives

$$\det(I-tAB)=\det(I-tBA).$$

Both sides are polynomials in $t$, so $AB$ and $BA$ have the same characteristic polynomial and hence the same eigenvalues, including algebraic multiplicities.

For part (II), let $v_i$ be eigenvectors of $A$ for its $n$ distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Since $AB=BA$,

$$A(Bv_i)=B(Av_i)=\lambda_iBv_i,$$

so $Bv_i$ lies in the one-dimensional eigenspace $\operatorname{span}(v_i)$. Thus $Bv_i=\mu_i v_i$. With $P=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$, both $P^{-1}AP$ and $P^{-1}BP$ are diagonal. In particular, $B$ is similar to a diagonal matrix.

## Answer

Because $A$ has three distinct eigenvalues, it is diagonalizable. Write $S^{-1}AS=D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$ and $C=S^{-1}BS$. Transforming $AB=2A-B$ gives

$$(D+I)C=2D.$$

Entrywise,

$$(\lambda_i+1)c_{ij}=2\lambda_i\delta_{ij}.$$

No $\lambda_i$ can equal $-1$, since the equation with $i=j$ would become $0=-2$. Hence $D+I$ is invertible and

$$C=2(D+I)^{-1}D=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{2\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+1},\frac{2\lambda_2}{\lambda_2+1},\frac{2\lambda_3}{\lambda_3+1}\right).$$

Therefore $C$ commutes with $D$, so $AB=BA$. The same invertible matrix $S$ diagonalizes both $A$ and $B$.

## Answer

Having $n$ distinct eigenvalues guarantees $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, so it is sufficient for diagonalizability. It is not necessary: for example, the identity matrix is already diagonal but has only one distinct eigenvalue.

Thus the condition is sufficient but not necessary: $\boxed{(B)}$.

## Answer

The statement that $A$ has eigenvalues $1,-1,0$ is equivalent here to $A$ being similar to

$$\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0).$$

That is precisely the existence of an invertible $P$ such that

$$A=P\Lambda P^{-1}.$$

The other choices describe equivalence, orthogonal similarity, or congruence and are not necessary for a general matrix. Hence $\boxed{(B)}$.

## Answer

If $A$ is diagonalizable, then $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $A^2=PD^2P^{-1}$, so diagonalizability of $A$ is sufficient. It is not necessary: take

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

This $A$ is not diagonalizable, while $A^2=0$ is diagonal. Therefore the condition is sufficient but not necessary: $\boxed{(A)}$.

## Answer

For a real $2\times2$ matrix, the characteristic discriminant is

$$\Delta=(a-d)^2+4bc.$$

If $\det A<0$, the two real eigenvalues have opposite signs and are distinct. If $b,c$ have the same sign, then $bc>0$ and $\Delta>0$. If $b=c$, then $A$ is real symmetric. Each of (A), (B), and (C) therefore guarantees diagonalizability.

Opposite signs for $b,c$ do not: for example $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no real eigenvalues and is not similar over $\mathbb R$ to a real diagonal matrix. Thus $\boxed{(D)}$ is not sufficient.

## Answer

If $P=(\alpha,A\alpha)$ were singular, then $A\alpha$ would be a scalar multiple of the nonzero vector $\alpha$, making $\alpha$ an eigenvector of $A$, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence $P$ is invertible.

In the basis $(\alpha,A\alpha)$,

$$A\alpha=A\alpha,\qquad A(A\alpha)=A^2\alpha=6\alpha-A\alpha,$$

so

$$P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}0&6\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+\lambda-6=(\lambda-2)(\lambda+3)$. The two eigenvalues are distinct, so $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix.

## Answer

Matrix (A) has the three distinct eigenvalues $1,2,-1$, while (B) is real symmetric. Matrix (D) has eigenvalues $1,2,2$, and for $\lambda=2$ its eigenspace is defined by one equation in three unknowns, so it has dimension two. All three are diagonalizable.

For (C), the leading $2\times2$ block

$$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$$

has the repeated eigenvalue $1$ but only one independent eigenvector. Consequently the full matrix cannot have three independent eigenvectors, regardless of $a$. The answer is $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

The equation is

$$A^2-A-2I=(A-2I)(A+I)=0.$$

The annihilating polynomial $(t-2)(t+1)$ has no repeated root, so the minimal polynomial of $A$ also has no repeated root. Therefore $A$ is diagonalizable. The equation does not force symmetry, $A=2I$, or the occurrence of eigenvalue $2$. Hence $\boxed{(C)}$.

## Answer

The eigenvalues of the leading $2\times2$ block are $6$ and $-2$, and the third diagonal entry is $6$. Thus $6$ has algebraic multiplicity two. Now

$$A-6I=\begin{pmatrix}-4&2&0\\8&-4&a\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

For the eigenspace of $6$ to have dimension two, this matrix must have rank one, which requires $a=0$. Then eigenvectors may be chosen as

$$v_1=(1,2,0)^T,\quad v_2=(0,0,1)^T \quad(\lambda=6),\qquad v_3=(1,-2,0)^T \quad(\lambda=-2).$$

Therefore one valid choice is

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\2&0&-2\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(6,6,-2).$$

So $\boxed{a=0}$.

## Answer

Write $A=(1-b)I+bJ$, where $J$ is the all-ones matrix. For $u=(1,\ldots,1)^T$,

$$Au=[1+(n-1)b]u.$$

Every vector $v$ satisfying $v_1+\cdots+v_n=0$ obeys $Jv=0$, so $Av=(1-b)v$. Thus the eigenvalues are

$$1+(n-1)b \quad(\text{once}),\qquad 1-b \quad(\text{multiplicity }n-1).$$

A basis of the second eigenspace is $e_1-e_n,\ldots,e_{n-1}-e_n$. Hence

$$P=(u,e_1-e_n,\ldots,e_{n-1}-e_n)$$

is invertible and

$$P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(1+(n-1)b,1-b,\ldots,1-b).$$

This remains valid when $b=0$.

## Answer

Similarity gives equality of characteristic polynomials. Direct calculation yields

$$\chi_A(\lambda)=\lambda^3-(a+3)\lambda^2+(3a-1)\lambda+3-2a,$$

$$\chi_B(\lambda)=\lambda^3-(b+2)\lambda^2+(2b+1)\lambda-b.$$

Comparing coefficients gives $\boxed{a=4,\ b=5}$. For these values, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $1,1,5$. Independent eigenvectors can be chosen as

$$v_1=(2,1,0)^T,\quad v_2=(-3,0,1)^T \quad(\lambda=1),\qquad v_3=(-1,-1,1)^T \quad(\lambda=5).$$

Thus

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}2&-3&-1\\1&0&-1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,5).$$

## Answer

Reading the coefficients of the displayed transformation gives

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&-1&1\\0&1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-2)(\lambda+1)(\lambda+2)$. Corresponding eigenvectors may be chosen as

$$v_{-2}=(0,-1,1)^T,\qquad v_{-1}=(-1,0,2)^T,\qquad v_2=(4,3,1)^T.$$

Therefore

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&4\\-1&0&3\\1&2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(-2,-1,2),$$

and $P^{-1}AP=\Lambda$.

## Answer

In the basis $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$, the matrix of $A$ is

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1&2&2\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its eigenvalues are $1,1,4$. Coordinate eigenvectors can be chosen as $(-1,1,0)^T$, $(-2,0,1)^T$, and $(0,1,1)^T$. Hence take

$$P=(-\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\ -2\alpha_1+\alpha_3,\ \alpha_2+\alpha_3).$$

These columns are independent, and

$$P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,4).$$

## Answer

The first row of $A$ is $(1,1,1)$. Applying it to the three given eigenvectors shows that their eigenvalues are respectively $3,2,1$. With

$$S=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$

we obtain

$$A=S\operatorname{diag}(3,2,1)S^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&2&1\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Since $A=SDS^{-1}$ and $A^T=S^{-T}DS^T$, the choice $P=SS^T$ satisfies $P^{-1}AP=A^T$. Explicitly,

$$P=\begin{pmatrix}3&2&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det P=1.$$

## Answer

In the basis $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$,

$$M=\begin{pmatrix}-1&4&-2\\-3&4&0\\-3&1&3\end{pmatrix}.$$

Its characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)$. Coordinate eigenvectors for $1,2,3$ may be chosen as $(1,1,1)^T$, $(2,3,3)^T$, and $(1,3,4)^T$. Therefore

$$P=(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3,\ 2\alpha_1+3\alpha_2+3\alpha_3,\ \alpha_1+3\alpha_2+4\alpha_3)$$

is invertible and $P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3)$. Since $6$ is not an eigenvalue, $A-6I$ is invertible, so

$$\boxed{\operatorname{rank}(A-6I)=3}.$$
